decks.title: Political Parties — Part 1: Why parties, and party systems
goals: Define a political party and name its three components
Describe the functions of political parties in a democracy
Explain why modern democracies need political parties
Compare one-party, two-party and multi-party systems and explain coalitions

slides.heading: Political Parties
slides.body_md: The most visible institution of democracy, and the one people complain about most. Why do we need parties at all?

nodes.label: What is a party?
What do parties do?
Why we need them
How many parties? Party systems

visual.alt: Route map of part 1: what a party is, what parties do, why democracies need them, and the kinds of party systems
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Namaste! At election time, you see flags, symbols, posters and rallies everywhere. These belong to political parties. People often criticise parties, and yet no large democracy works without them. In this part, we find out what a party is, what it does, why we cannot do without it, and how many parties a democracy should have.

slides.heading: What is a political party?
slides.body_md: A **political party** is an organisation of people who **share ideas about policy** and **contest elections** to win power in government. Because it speaks for one section or viewpoint, a party is **partisan**.

nodes.label: Political party
Leaders: decide policy and lead campaigns
Active members: work for the party
Followers: support and vote for it

visual.alt: Tree of the three components of a political party: leaders who decide policy, active members who work for the party, and followers who support it

slides.narration: A political party is a group of people who agree on certain policies and try to win elections so that they can put those policies into action. Every party has three parts: leaders at the top, active members who do the work, and followers who support it. A party always takes a side on issues. That is why we call it partisan.

slides.heading: Quick check: what is a party?
slides.body_md: Which of the following best describes a **political party**?
slides.narration: Look for shared policies and the aim of winning elections.

slides.heading: Seven functions of parties

rows: Offer voters a few clear packages to choose from
Members vote in legislatures, usually as the party directs
The winning party leads the executive
Losing parties criticise and check the government
Raise issues, run campaigns and movements
Local leaders help people reach offices and welfare schemes

visual.alt: Table of seven functions of political parties: contesting elections, offering policies, making laws, forming governments, acting as opposition, shaping public opinion, and giving people access to government machinery and welfare schemes

slides.narration: Parties do much more than fight elections. They choose candidates, offer policy choices, make laws, form governments, and when they lose, they act as the opposition. They also raise issues and shape public opinion. And for ordinary people, a local party leader is often the easiest way to reach a government office or a welfare scheme.

slides.heading: Choosing candidates: India and the USA

rows: Party members and supporters take part (primaries)

visual.alt: Table comparing candidate selection: in most Indian parties top leaders choose candidates, while in the USA party members and supporters take part through primaries

slides.narration: How are candidates chosen? In most Indian parties, the top leaders decide who gets a ticket. In the United States, members and supporters of a party take part in choosing candidates through what are called primaries. Keep this difference in mind. It will matter when we discuss the challenge of internal democracy in part two.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: name the function
slides.body_md: Question: *Name the function in each: (a) a party worker helps a widow apply for a pension; (b) a losing party walks out of the assembly to protest a new tax; (c) a party publishes a plan for free school meals before an election.* (3 × 1)
bullets: Step 1 — Ask who benefits and how.
Step 2 — (a) **access to government machinery and welfare schemes**.
Step 3 — (b) **acting as the opposition**.
Step 4 — (c) **putting forward policies and programmes**.

rows: Helps a citizen reach a scheme
Protests in the legislature after losing

visual.alt: Table matching clues to functions: helping a citizen reach a scheme is access to government, protesting after losing is opposition, publishing a plan is policies and programmes

slides.narration: In situation questions, look for the clue. Helping a person reach a government scheme is access. Criticising or protesting after losing is opposition. A plan before the election is a policy programme. Write the function in the exact words you learnt, then one phrase from the situation as proof.

slides.heading: Why do we need parties?
slides.body_md: Parties arose **along with representative democracy**: large societies need a way to bring representatives together around policies.

nodes.label: Imagine: every candidate is an independent
Each winner pushes only for their own area
Each member answers only to a constituency
A government forms, but no one is responsible for it
So: parties are needed for responsible government

visual.alt: Flow of a thought experiment: if every candidate were independent, each winner would push only for their own area, nobody could carry out a national programme, and there would be no group to blame or replace; so parties are needed

slides.narration: Try a thought experiment. Suppose every candidate stood as an independent. Each would promise things for their own area, but no one could promise to change national policy. A government would form, but who would be responsible for it? Nobody. Parties solve this problem. They bring representatives together around a programme, so voters know whom to reward or punish.

slides.heading: Quick check: components of a party
slides.body_md: The three components of a political party are…
slides.narration: Think of the people at the top, the people who work, and the people who support.

slides.heading: Party systems

rows: Only one party may rule; no free competition
Two big parties take turns in power; smaller ones win a handful of seats
Three or more parties can realistically govern, alone or together

visual.alt: Table of party systems: one-party systems allow only one party to rule, as in China; two-party systems see two big parties take turns, as in the USA and UK; multi-party systems let several parties compete, as in India

slides.narration: How many parties should a democracy have? Countries differ. In China, only one party is allowed to rule, so voters have no real choice. In the United States and the United Kingdom, two main parties usually take turns. In India, many parties compete, and several can come to power alone or in alliance. That is a multi-party system.

slides.heading: Why a one-party system is not democratic
slides.body_md: Democracy needs **at least two parties** competing fairly, so that power can change hands.

rows: Can voters choose among real alternatives?
Can those in power be voted out?

visual.alt: Table testing a one-party system against democratic tests: voters cannot choose real alternatives, rulers cannot be voted out, and opponents cannot organise freely

slides.narration: A one-party system may look orderly, but it fails the basic tests of democracy. Voters cannot choose among real alternatives. Those in power cannot be voted out. Opponents cannot organise freely. That is why a one-party system fails as a democracy. Democracy needs competition.

slides.heading: Alliances and coalitions
slides.body_md: An **alliance** or **front**: several parties that fight an election together and share power if they win.

nodes.label: Many parties contest
No single party wins a majority
Parties form an alliance or front
They agree on a common programme
A coalition government is formed

visual.alt: Flow: many parties contest, no single party wins a majority, parties form an alliance, agree on a common programme and form a coalition government

slides.narration: In a multi-party system, it often happens that no single party wins a majority. Then parties join hands in an alliance, sometimes called a front. They agree on a common programme and form a coalition government. In India, coalition governments ruled at the centre for long periods after nineteen eighty-nine. Coalitions can include national and state parties.

slides.heading: Quick check: alliances
slides.body_md: Several parties agree to fight an election together and to share power if they win. Such a grouping is called…
slides.narration: Think of a word that means joining together, or a common battle line.

slides.heading: Multi-party systems: messy but representative
columns:
**Merits**

Many groups, regions and viewpoints get a voice. Smaller groups can bargain for their concerns. Power is shared among more parties.

**Drawbacks**

Coalitions may fall if a partner withdraws. Partners with different programmes may disagree and slow decisions. Voters may find it confusing.

visual.alt: Table of merits and drawbacks of a multi-party system: many voices and regional concerns are represented, but there can be instability and slower decisions

slides.narration: Multi-party systems often look messy. Coalitions can fall when a partner walks out, and partners may argue. But they also let many interests and regions be heard, which matters in a diverse country. In an exam, never call one system simply good or bad. Weigh the merits against the drawbacks, and connect them to the country's society.

slides.heading: Why India has many parties
slides.body_md: No country **chooses** its party system in one go; it **evolves** over a long time.

nodes.label: Large social and regional diversity
History and the national movement
Electoral system
Multi-party system

visual.alt: Flow: social and regional diversity, history and the electoral system together produce India's multi-party system

slides.narration: Why does India have so many parties? India is very diverse, with many languages, regions and social groups, and two or three parties cannot easily represent them all. History and the electoral system matter too. No country simply picks a party system; it grows out of the society over a long time. The best system for one country may not suit another.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: classify party systems from data
slides.body_md: Question: *In Country A, two parties have won about 95 of 100 seats in every election, taking turns in power. In Country B, six parties win seats and the largest has 31. Classify each and say how B is likely to be governed.* (3 marks)
bullets: Step 1 — A: power alternates between **two** parties → **two-party system**.
Step 2 — B: many parties, none near 51 → **multi-party system**.
Step 3 — B will need an **alliance** → **coalition government**.

rows: Two parties take turns; others tiny
Many parties; largest far below half

visual.alt: Table: two parties taking turns means a two-party system; many parties with none near half means a multi-party system; no majority means a coalition

slides.narration: With seat data, two numbers matter: how many parties win seats, and whether any one reaches half. If two parties take turns and others are tiny, it is two-party. If many parties win seats and none gets close to half, it is multi-party, and a coalition is likely. Write the inference with the number that proves it.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a 5-mark answer on functions
slides.body_md: Question: *Describe the functions of political parties.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Pick five of the seven functions.
Step 2 — For each, one line of meaning, ideally with a tiny example.
Step 3 — Combine the less-asked ones (opinion and access) in the last point.
Step 4 — Avoid naming present-day parties; use general examples.

rows: Form government or act as opposition
Shape opinion; give access to schemes

visual.alt: Marking plan: one mark each for contesting elections, policies and programmes, law-making, government or opposition, and shaping opinion with access to schemes

slides.narration: This is the most common long question in the chapter. The easiest plan is five functions, one line each. Notice how two smaller functions can share the last line, which saves words. And keep examples general, like a party campaigning on water shortage. Examiners do not need, and do not reward, comments about real parties.

slides.heading: Quick check: one-party systems
slides.body_md: In which country does a single party control the government, with no free competition for power?
slides.narration: Which of these countries does not allow other parties to compete for power?

slides.heading: Summary

rows: People who share policies and contest elections; partisan; leaders, active members, followers
Contest elections; policies; laws; government or opposition; public opinion; access to schemes
Without parties: no policy programmes, no responsible government
Alliances form when no party has a majority; representative but can be unstable

visual.alt: Summary table: definition of a party, its functions, why parties are needed, party systems and coalitions

slides.narration: To sum up: a party is a group that shares policies and contests elections. It has leaders, active members and followers. Parties contest elections, offer policies, make laws, form governments or oppose them, shape opinion and connect people to the government. Democracy needs them. Party systems may be one-party, two-party or multi-party, and India's diversity has made it multi-party, with frequent coalitions.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Learn **seven functions**; a 5-mark answer needs five.
Give **examples** of each party system: China; USA and UK; India.
Say why a one-party system is **not democratic**: no choice, no change of power.
For multi-party systems, give **both** merits and drawbacks.
Never praise or criticise a real party or leader in your answers.
slides.narration: Some final tips. Learn all seven functions so you can pick five. Know one example of each party system. Explain clearly why one-party rule is not democratic. Balance merits and drawbacks for multi-party systems. And stay neutral: your answers should be about how parties work, not about which party you like.

decks.title: Political Parties — Part 2: Recognised parties, challenges and reforms
goals: State the Election Commission criteria for recognition of state and national parties
Describe major national parties and the rise of state parties neutrally
Evaluate the challenges facing political parties
Explain reforms already made and suggest further reforms, with their limits

slides.heading: Parties in India
slides.body_md: Who counts as a national party? What is wrong with parties, and how can they be fixed?

nodes.label: Registration and recognition
National and state parties
Challenges
Reforms made and suggested

visual.alt: Route map of part 2: registration and recognition, national and state parties, challenges, and reforms made and suggested
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: India has a very large number of registered political parties. Only some of them are recognised by the Election Commission as national or state parties. In this part, we learn the rules for recognition, look briefly at major parties in a neutral way, and then study the real problems parties face and the reforms that have been tried or proposed.

slides.heading: Registration and recognition

nodes.label: Every party registers with the Election Commission
Parties that meet the criteria are recognised
Recognised parties get a reserved symbol and other facilities
Only official candidates may use the symbol

visual.alt: Flow: every party registers with the Election Commission; those that meet criteria are recognised; recognised parties get a reserved symbol and other facilities; only their official candidates may use it

slides.narration: Every party in India must register with the Election Commission. Bigger, established parties that meet certain criteria are recognised. A recognised party gets a symbol reserved for it alone, and some other facilities. Symbols matter in a country where many voters recognise a picture faster than a name.

slides.heading: The criteria (as given in the syllabus)
slides.body_md: Both conditions, **votes and seats**, must be met. The Commission's full rules include some alternative routes; learn these as the syllabus states them.

rows: At least 6% of the votes in a state assembly election
At least 2 seats in that assembly
At least 6% of the votes in Lok Sabha elections, or in assembly elections in four states
At least 4 seats in the Lok Sabha

visual.alt: Table of recognition criteria: a state party needs at least 6 per cent of votes and 2 seats in a state assembly election; a national party needs at least 6 per cent of votes in Lok Sabha elections or in assembly elections in four states, and at least 4 Lok Sabha seats

slides.narration: Here are the criteria as your syllabus gives them. A state party needs at least six per cent of the votes in a state assembly election and at least two seats. A national party needs at least six per cent of the votes in Lok Sabha elections, or in assembly elections in four states, and at least four Lok Sabha seats. Remember: votes and seats, both.

slides.heading: Quick check: state-party criteria
slides.body_md: A party is recognised as a **state party** if it…
slides.narration: Two conditions: a vote share and a number of seats in one state.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: apply the criteria
slides.body_md: Question: *Party P won 7% of the votes and 1 seat in a state assembly election; Party Q won 6.5% of the Lok Sabha vote and 5 Lok Sabha seats. Which qualifies, and as what?* (2 marks)
bullets: Step 1 — P, state test: 7% ≥ 6% ✓; 1 seat < 2 ✗ → **does not qualify**.
Step 2 — Q, national test: 6.5% ≥ 6% ✓; 5 seats ≥ 4 ✓ → **national party**.
Step 3 — Write each condition with its number.

visual.alt: Table: party P meets the votes test but not the seats test and is not recognised; party Q meets both national tests and is a national party

slides.narration: Treat recognition like a two-key lock. Check the votes key, then the seats key, and write both checks with the numbers. Party P has the votes but not the seats, so it fails. Party Q has both, so it qualifies as a national party. Students lose marks by checking only one condition.

slides.heading: Major national parties: a neutral snapshot
slides.body_md: The Election Commission **revises** the list of recognised parties after elections; check its latest notification for the current list. Each party sets out its own ideology in its constitution and manifesto.

rows: Led much of the freedom movement; led governments at the centre for long periods after independence
Grew out of the Bharatiya Jana Sangh (1951); has led governments at the centre in several periods
Formed after a split in the Communist Party of India; has led governments in some states

visual.alt: Table of three parties that have long held national recognition: the Indian National Congress, founded 1885; the Bharatiya Janata Party, founded 1980 from the Bharatiya Jana Sangh; and the Communist Party of India (Marxist), founded 1964

slides.narration: Here are three parties that have long held national recognition, with their founding years. We describe them by history only. Each party explains its own ideas in its constitution and manifesto, and you can read them there. Remember that the Election Commission reviews recognition after elections, so the full list of national parties changes. Always check its latest notification.

slides.heading: The rise of state parties
slides.body_md: A "state" party is defined by **where its support lies**; it also takes positions on **national** issues.

rows: State (regional) parties grew stronger in many states
Regional concerns gained a louder voice
They joined coalitions at the centre
The centre consulted states more; federalism strengthened
More parties in the Lok Sabha

visual.alt: Table: state parties grew stronger, joined coalitions at the centre and made the Lok Sabha more diverse, giving regional concerns a louder voice and strengthening federalism

slides.narration: Over the last few decades, state parties, often called regional parties, have grown stronger in many states. Many have led state governments, and several have been partners in coalitions at the centre. This gave regional concerns a louder voice and made the centre consult the states more. It links directly to what you learnt in Federalism.

slides.heading: Quick check: party symbols
slides.body_md: What special facility does a **recognised** party get from the Election Commission?
slides.narration: Think of what you see on a voting machine next to each name.

slides.heading: Four challenges to parties

rows: No members' register, no internal elections; a few leaders decide everything
Top posts pass within one family; long-serving workers are passed over
Tickets for those who can spend heavily or intimidate; donors seek influence
Major parties offer similar policies; leaders switch parties

visual.alt: Table of four challenges: lack of internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, and lack of meaningful choice, each with what it looks like

slides.narration: Why do people lose faith in parties? There are four big challenges. Many parties have little internal democracy: no member lists, no internal elections. In some, top posts pass within a family. Money and muscle power influence who gets tickets. And when major parties offer similar policies and leaders switch sides, voters feel they have no meaningful choice.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: identify the challenge
slides.body_md: Question: *A party worker writes: "There is no list of members, the ticket went to the president's nephew, and another party picks candidates by how much they can spend." Name the challenges.* (3 marks)
bullets: Step 1 — "No list of members" → **lack of internal democracy**.
Step 2 — "President's nephew" → **dynastic succession**.
Step 3 — "How much they can spend" → **money power**.

rows: Picked by how much they can spend

visual.alt: Table matching phrases to challenges: no list of members is lack of internal democracy, the nephew's ticket is dynastic succession, and spending power is money power

slides.narration: This is a typical source question. Underline each phrase that hints at a problem, then name the challenge in the exact words of the syllabus. One phrase, one challenge, one mark. If part c asks for reforms, match each reform to one of these challenges.

slides.heading: Reforms already made

rows: An elected member who changes party loses the seat
Members must follow the leadership, which makes leaders more powerful
Candidates declare property and pending criminal cases
Information helps only if voters use it
Parties must hold organisational elections and file income tax returns
Internal elections can be a formality

visual.alt: Table of reforms: the anti-defection law makes a member who changes party lose the seat but strengthens leaders; affidavits disclose property and criminal cases but help only if voters use them; the Election Commission order requires organisational elections and tax returns but these can be a formality

slides.narration: Some reforms have already been made. The anti-defection law of nineteen eighty-five means an elected member who switches party loses the seat. It reduced defections but made party leaders more powerful. Candidates must now declare their property and criminal cases in an affidavit. And parties must hold organisational elections and file tax returns. Each reform helps, but each has limits.

slides.heading: Quick check: the anti-defection law
slides.body_md: Under the anti-defection law, what happens to an elected MP or MLA who changes party after the election?
slides.narration: What would stop a member from switching sides for a reward?

slides.heading: Reforms suggested

nodes.label: Suggested reforms
Law on internal democracy: members' register, party constitution, open elections, independent dispute authority
A minimum share of tickets for women, and women in party decision bodies
State funding of elections: help in kind or cash linked to votes
Pressure from citizens, media and movements; more people joining parties

visual.alt: Tree of suggested reforms: a law on internal democracy, a minimum share of tickets for women, state funding of elections, and pressure and participation by citizens

slides.narration: Many further reforms have been proposed. A law could require parties to keep member registers and hold open internal elections. Parties could give a minimum share of tickets to women. The state could fund part of election costs, so candidates depend less on rich donors. And citizens, the media and movements can push parties to change, especially if more good people join them.

slides.heading: Careful: reform without over-control
slides.body_md: The best reforms **increase participation and transparency** without giving any government power to **control its opponents**.

rows: The ruling party may misuse laws against rivals
People may be discouraged from politics

visual.alt: Table: too little regulation leaves parties closed and money-driven and voters lose trust; too much regulation may be misused against rivals and discourage people from politics

slides.narration: Reform needs balance. If parties are not regulated at all, they may stay closed and dominated by money. But if the law controls every detail, the party in power could use it to harm its rivals, and people might stay away from politics. Good reforms open parties to members and make them transparent, without handing any government a weapon against its opponents.

slides.heading: Reading a chart: imagined party data
slides.body_md: Imagined figures: Party X fields the **fewest women** and the **most** candidates with pending serious criminal cases.

series.label: Candidates with pending serious criminal cases

x.label: Imagined party (1 W, 2 X, 3 Y, 4 Z)

y.label: Per cent of the party's candidates

visual.alt: Bar chart of four imagined parties: women candidates 30, 8, 12 and 18 per cent; candidates with pending serious criminal cases 2, 15, 9 and 4 per cent
visual.caption: Imagined figures for parties W, X, Y and Z.

slides.narration: This chart uses imagined figures for four parties. For each party, the first bar shows the share of women among its candidates, and the second shows the share with pending serious criminal cases. Party W does best on both measures; Party X does worst. In an exam, compare with numbers, then link each figure to a challenge and a reform.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a 5-mark evaluation of reforms
slides.body_md: Question: *What efforts have been made to reform parties? Suggest further reforms and evaluate their limits.* (about 120 words)
bullets: Step 1 — Three reforms made: anti-defection law, affidavits, EC order on organisational elections and tax returns.
Step 2 — One line each on **effect and limit**.
Step 3 — Suggestions: internal-democracy law, tickets for women, state funding.
Step 4 — End with balance: avoid over-regulation; public pressure matters.

visual.alt: Marking plan: anti-defection law with its side-effect, affidavits, the Election Commission order, suggested reforms, and limits with public pressure

slides.narration: An evaluation needs judgement, not just a list. For each reform, say what it does and one limit. Then suggest improvements. Finish with the big idea: laws alone cannot fix parties, and over-regulation is risky, so citizens' pressure and participation are essential. That final balance usually earns the top mark.

slides.heading: Quick check: affidavits
slides.body_md: Following a Supreme Court order, what must every candidate file before contesting an election?
slides.narration: It is a sworn statement about the candidate's property and court cases.

slides.heading: Summary

rows: Registered with the Election Commission; recognised parties get a reserved symbol
State: 6% of votes + 2 assembly seats. National: 6% in Lok Sabha or four states + 4 Lok Sabha seats
Congress (1885), BJP (1980), CPI(M) (1964) long recognised; list revised after elections; state parties stronger
Internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, meaningful choice
Anti-defection law (1985), affidavits, EC order; suggested: internal-democracy law, women's tickets, state funding, public pressure

visual.alt: Summary table: recognition, criteria, parties, challenges and reforms

slides.narration: To sum up. Parties register with the Election Commission, and those meeting the vote-and-seat criteria are recognised as state or national parties, with reserved symbols. The list changes after elections. Parties face four challenges: weak internal democracy, dynastic succession, money and muscle power, and a lack of meaningful choice. Some reforms have been made, more are proposed, and citizens' pressure remains the key.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Recognition questions: check **both** votes and seats, and show the numbers.
Do not state how many national parties exist "today"; the list changes.
Learn the **four challenges** and match each to a **reform**.
For the anti-defection law, mention its **side-effect** on party leaders.
Stay neutral: describe parties by **history and rules**, not by opinion.
slides.narration: Final tips. In recognition questions, test both votes and seats and write the numbers. Avoid stating how many national parties exist today, because the list changes. Learn the four challenges and pair each with a reform. Mention the side-effect of the anti-defection law. And stay neutral: describe parties by their history and rules, never by your opinion of them.

notes.title: Political Parties — Notes

sections.heading: 1. What a party is and what it does
sections.body_md:
A **political party** is an organisation of people who **share ideas about policy** and **contest elections** to win power in government. It speaks for one section or viewpoint, so it is **partisan**. Three components: **leaders**, **active members**, **followers**.

**Functions**
1. **Contest elections.** In most Indian parties, top leaders choose candidates; in the USA, members and supporters take part through primaries.
2. **Put forward policies and programmes**, offering voters a few clear packages to choose from; the winning party's policies guide the government.
3. **Make laws:** members in legislatures debate and usually vote as the party directs.
4. **Form and run governments.**
5. **Act as the opposition:** criticise the government, expose failures, mobilise people.
6. **Shape public opinion:** raise issues, run campaigns and movements.
7. **Give access** to government machinery and **welfare schemes** through local leaders.

key_terms.definition_md: An organisation of people who share policy goals and contest elections to win power in government.
Taking a side; speaking for one section or viewpoint.

rows: A plan for farm prices or school meals
Voting on a bill as a party
Campaigns on water; helping people reach schemes

visual.alt: Table of the functions of parties with examples

sections.heading: 2. Why democracies need parties
sections.body_md: Without parties, every candidate would be an **independent**. Each winner would push only for **their own area**; nobody could carry out a **national programme**; and when things went wrong there would be **no group to blame or replace**. Parties bring representatives together around a programme, so voters know whom to hold **accountable**. The rise of parties is linked to the rise of **representative democracy**.

key_terms.definition_md: Being answerable to the people for decisions and their results.

nodes.label: All candidates independent
No national programme
No one responsible for the government
Parties needed

visual.alt: Flow showing why democracy needs parties

sections.heading: 3. Party systems
sections.body_md:
- **One-party system:** only one party may control the government; no free competition (e.g. **China**). It fails as a democracy: no choice, no change of power.
- **Two-party system:** two big parties **take turns** in power; smaller parties may win a handful of seats but do not govern (e.g. **USA, United Kingdom**).
- **Multi-party system:** three or more parties can realistically govern, alone or by **teaming up** (e.g. **India**).

An **alliance** or **front** is formed when several parties agree to fight an election together and share power; if it wins, it forms a **coalition government**. Multi-party systems let many **interests and regions** be represented but can be **unstable**, since coalitions may fall.

No country simply **chooses** its party system; it **evolves** with the society's divisions, history and electoral system. India's social and regional **diversity** has produced a multi-party system.

key_terms.definition_md: A group of parties that fight an election together and share power if they win.
A government formed by two or more parties together.

visual.alt: Table of party systems with examples

sections.heading: 4. National and state parties
sections.body_md:
Every party **registers** with the **Election Commission**. Parties that meet set criteria are **recognised** and get a **unique reserved symbol** (reserved for them alone on the ballot) and some other facilities.

**Criteria as given in the syllabus**
- **State party:** at least **6%** of the votes in a state assembly election **and** at least **2 seats**.
- **National party:** at least **6%** of the votes in **Lok Sabha** elections or in assembly elections in **four states**, **and** at least **4 Lok Sabha seats**.
(The Commission's full rules include some alternative routes.)

The Commission **reviews** recognition after elections, so the list changes; check its latest notification. Parties that have long held national recognition include the **Indian National Congress** (founded **1885**; led much of the freedom movement), the **Bharatiya Janata Party** (founded **1980**, from the Bharatiya Jana Sangh of 1951) and the **Communist Party of India (Marxist)** (formed **1964**). Each sets out its ideology in its own constitution and manifesto.

**State parties** have grown stronger since the 1990s; many have led state governments and joined coalitions at the centre, giving regional concerns a louder voice.

sections.heading: 5. Challenges and reforms
sections.body_md:
**Challenges**
1. **Lack of internal democracy:** many keep **no list of members** and hold **no internal elections**, so a **small group at the top** takes the decisions.
2. **Dynastic succession:** top posts pass within **one family**; members without family links are passed over.
3. **Money and muscle power:** tickets for those who can **spend heavily** or have **criminal** influence; donors may seek influence over policy.
4. **Lack of meaningful choice:** policy differences between major parties have **narrowed**; leaders **switch** parties.

**Reforms already made**
- **Anti-defection law** (constitutional amendment, **1985**): an elected member who changes party **loses the seat**; it has also made party **leaders more powerful**.
- **Affidavits:** after a Supreme Court order, candidates declare **property** and pending **criminal cases**.
- **Election Commission order:** parties must hold **organisational elections** and file **income tax returns**.

**Suggested reforms:** a **law on internal democracy** (members' register, party constitution, open elections, an independent authority to settle disputes); a minimum share of **tickets for women** and women in decision bodies; **state funding** of elections (in kind or in cash linked to votes). **Caution:** over-regulation could be **misused** by the ruling party against rivals. **Public pressure** (petitions, media, movements) and **more citizens joining parties** are essential.

A signed statement made on oath and submitted to an official.
Passing top party posts to members of one family.

rows: Members' register and open internal elections
Affidavits; denying tickets to those facing serious charges

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Checking only one condition for recognition: **votes and seats** are both needed.
- Stating a fixed number of national parties "today": the Election Commission **revises** the list after elections.
- Calling a one-party system democratic because it is stable: there is **no choice** and **no change of power**.
- Listing reforms without their **limits** in an evaluation question (e.g. the anti-defection law strengthens leaders).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark MCQ and assertion-reason: one correct option.
- 2 marks: two points (about 40 words); 3 marks: three points (about 60 words).
- 5 marks: five distinct points (about 120 words); evaluations need a judgement.
- Source and case items (4): 1 + 1 + 2; in recognition cases, show each number against its criterion.

**Tone.** Describe parties by history and rules; do not praise or criticise any present-day party or leader.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following best describes a **political party**?

options.text_md: Any group of people who live in the same area
A group that only protests and never contests elections
A government department that runs elections
An organisation of people who agree on certain policies and seek to win elections and hold power in government

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A party brings together people with shared ideas about policy.
Step 2: Its aim is to contest elections and form or influence the government, so (d). (c) describes the Election Commission; (b) describes some movements.

questions.stem_md: The three components of a political party are

options.text_md: the Election Commission, candidates and voters
the union, state and local governments

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A party has leaders at the top, active members who work for it, and followers who support it.
Step 2: So (a).

questions.stem_md: Why is a political party described as "partisan"?

options.text_md: Because it is part of the government
Because it is banned from elections
Because it stands for one section or viewpoint in society and takes a side on issues

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A party is a part of society, not the whole of it.
Step 2: It takes a side and speaks for a particular view or section, so it is partisan: (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is **not** a function of political parties in a democracy?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Parties contest elections, offer policies, make laws, form governments, act as opposition, shape opinion and help people reach government schemes.
Step 2: Deciding court cases is the job of the judiciary, so (c).

questions.stem_md: How are candidates chosen in most Indian parties, compared with the USA?

options.text_md: In India, voters of the whole country choose them; in the USA, the President does.
In both, candidates are chosen by lottery.
In both, the Election Commission chooses them.
In India, top party leaders usually choose them; in the USA, party members and supporters take part in choosing them.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: In India, candidates are usually selected by the party's top leaders.
Step 2: In the USA, members and supporters of a party take part in choosing its candidates through primaries. So (d).

questions.stem_md: A party loses the election. What role does it play in a democracy?

options.text_md: It must stop all political work until the next election.
It acts as the opposition: it questions the government, criticises failures and puts forward other views.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Parties that lose remain in the legislature and in public life.
Step 2: As the opposition, they hold the government to account and mobilise people on issues, so (d).

questions.stem_md: A villager who cannot get her ration card goes to a local party worker, who helps her approach the right office. Which function of parties is this?

options.text_md: Giving people access to government machinery and welfare schemes

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The party worker links an ordinary citizen with the government office.
Step 2: That is the function of providing access to government machinery and welfare schemes, so (d).

questions.stem_md: A party organises meetings and campaigns across a state to raise awareness about water shortage. Which function is it performing?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The party raises an issue and builds public awareness.
Step 2: That is shaping public opinion, so (a). Parties also launch movements on such issues.

questions.stem_md: Most members of a legislature vote on a bill as their party directs. Which statement explains this?

options.text_md: Laws are made by the courts.
Members have no right to speak.
Members are bound by their party's decisions, so parties largely decide how laws are made.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Laws are debated and passed in the legislature.
Step 2: Most members belong to parties and follow the party line, so parties shape law-making: (c).

questions.stem_md: Imagine a country where every candidate contests as an independent. What is the most likely problem?

options.text_md: There would be too many policies to choose from.
The courts would form the government.
Nobody could carry out a national programme, and there would be no group to blame or replace when things went wrong.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: An independent member answers only to a constituency and cannot carry out a national programme alone.
Step 2: The government would be formed, but no group would be accountable for its policies, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Political parties grew up along with the spread of which form of government?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Large societies need representatives, and representatives need a way to organise around policies.
Step 2: Parties arose along with representative democracies, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Party A promises to raise the minimum support price for crops; Party B promises lower taxes on small businesses. How does this help voters?

options.text_md: It confuses voters, so they should not vote.
Voters can choose among different policy packages, which is a key function of parties.
It means the courts will decide which policy is better.
It shows that parties never keep promises.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Parties offer voters a few clear packages of policies.
Step 2: Voters then choose the package they prefer, so (b).

questions.stem_md: In which country does a single party control the government, with no free competition for power?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: China is run by the Communist Party of China; other parties cannot compete to replace it.
Step 2: So (b). India has a multi-party system; the UK and USA are usually described as two-party systems.

questions.stem_md: Why does a one-party system **fail** as a democracy?

options.text_md: Voters have no real choice, and the ruling party cannot be voted out.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Democracy needs at least two parties competing so that power can change hands.
Step 2: In a one-party system there is no fair chance for others to win, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Which statement describes a **two-party** system?

options.text_md: Only two parties are legally allowed to exist.
Two parties always rule together in a coalition.
Power usually changes hands between two main parties, though smaller parties may exist and win a few seats.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Other parties are allowed, but only two have a serious chance of winning a majority.
Step 2: So (d). The UK and the USA are usual examples.

questions.stem_md: In a country, three or more parties can realistically hope to govern, either alone or by teaming up with others. This is a
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Several serious contenders for power define a multi-party system.
Step 2: So (c). India is an example.

questions.stem_md: Several parties agree to fight an election together and to share power if they win. Such a grouping is called
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Parties that agree to contest together form an alliance or front.
Step 2: If they win, they form a coalition government. So (b).

questions.stem_md: Which is an **advantage** of a multi-party system?

options.text_md: It always produces a single-party majority.
It prevents regional parties from forming.
It gives many different groups and viewpoints a voice in government.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: More parties mean more groups and regions find a voice.
Step 2: So (d). The cost is that governments can be less stable.

questions.stem_md: Why has India developed a multi-party system?

options.text_md: The Constitution allows only many small parties.
The Election Commission chose it in 1950.
India's social and regional diversity is too great for two parties to represent all of it.
Voters are not allowed to vote for large parties.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A party system grows out of a society's divisions, history and electoral system; no country simply picks one.
Step 2: India's many social and regional groups have produced many parties, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about party systems is correct?

options.text_md: Every country chooses its party system by a vote.
There is one ideal party system that suits all countries.
A party system grows slowly out of a country's own society, history and way of holding elections.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: No country selects its party system in one decision; it develops gradually.
Step 2: Its shape depends on social and regional divisions, history and the electoral system, so (c). There is no single ideal system.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined country, the last five elections were won alternately by Party X and Party Y; small parties together never won more than 6 per cent of seats. The country has
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Power moves between two main parties; others exist but are not serious contenders.
Step 2: That is a two-party system, so (b).

questions.stem_md: A coalition government falls when one partner withdraws support. Which feature of multi-party systems does this show?

options.text_md: It can sometimes lead to political instability.
It always gives one party a majority.
It prevents opposition parties from existing.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Coalitions depend on agreement among partners.
Step 2: When a partner leaves, the government may fall, so multi-party systems can seem messy and unstable: (a).

questions.stem_md: Which body registers political parties in India?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Every party must register with the Election Commission.
Step 2: The Commission also recognises some parties and gives them reserved symbols, so (d).

questions.stem_md: What special facility does a **recognised** party get from the Election Commission?

options.text_md: A symbol reserved for it alone, which no other candidate may use

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Recognition gives a party a reserved election symbol and some other facilities.
Step 2: Only that party's official candidates may use the symbol, so (b).

questions.stem_md: According to the Election Commission criteria as given in the syllabus, a party is recognised as a **state party** if it

options.text_md: wins one seat in the Lok Sabha
gets at least 6 per cent of the votes in a state assembly election and wins at least 2 seats
is more than ten years old

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The criterion combines votes and seats in a state assembly election.
Step 2: At least 6 per cent of the votes and at least 2 seats, so (b).

questions.stem_md: According to the criteria given in the syllabus, a party is recognised as a **national party** if it

options.text_md: wins elections in one large state
has its office in New Delhi
gets at least 6 per cent of the total votes in Lok Sabha elections or in assembly elections in four states, and wins at least 4 Lok Sabha seats

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The test is spread across the country plus seats in the Lok Sabha.
Step 2: At least 6 per cent of votes in Lok Sabha elections or in assembly elections in four states, and at least 4 Lok Sabha seats, so (c).

questions.stem_md: In a state assembly election, Party P wins 8 per cent of the votes but only 1 seat. Under the criteria in the syllabus, Party P

options.text_md: becomes a state party because its vote share is above 6 per cent
does not qualify, because it needs at least 2 seats as well

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Both conditions must be met: at least 6 per cent of votes and at least 2 seats.
Step 2: P has the votes but only 1 seat, so it does not qualify: (b). Registration is a separate matter.

questions.stem_md: Party Q won 7 per cent of the total votes in the Lok Sabha election and 5 Lok Sabha seats. Under the criteria in the syllabus, Party Q

options.text_md: qualifies only as a state party
must first win a state election

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: National party test: at least 6 per cent of Lok Sabha votes (7 per cent: met) and at least 4 Lok Sabha seats (5: met).
Step 2: Both met, so (a).

questions.stem_md: Which national party was founded in 1885 and played a central role in India's freedom movement?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885.
Step 2: It led much of the national movement, so (a). The BJP was founded in 1980 and the CPI(M) in 1964.

questions.stem_md: In which year was the Bharatiya Janata Party founded?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The BJP was founded in 1980, drawing on the Bharatiya Jana Sangh formed in 1951.
Step 2: So (c).

questions.stem_md: The Communist Party of India (Marxist) was founded in
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The CPI(M) was formed in 1964.
Step 2: So (b).

questions.stem_md: Why does the list of recognised national and state parties change from time to time?

options.text_md: The Constitution fixes the list every year.
The President chooses new parties every year.
The Election Commission reviews recognition after elections, based on each party's votes and seats.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Recognition depends on electoral performance.
Step 2: After elections, the Commission reviews which parties meet the criteria, so the list changes, (d).

questions.stem_md: Which development has made the Lok Sabha more diverse since the 1990s?

options.text_md: The growing strength of state (regional) parties and their role in coalitions at the centre
The end of elections in the states

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: State parties grew stronger and many joined coalitions at the centre.
Step 2: This brought more regional voices into national politics, so (b).

questions.stem_md: A party that is recognised as a state party has its strongest base in one state, but it also has views on national issues. What does this show?

options.text_md: State parties are not allowed to discuss national issues.
A "state" or regional party is defined by where its support lies, not by an inability to think nationally.
It must be a national party.
It cannot contest Lok Sabha elections.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Recognition as a state party reflects where a party wins its votes and seats.
Step 2: Such parties contest Lok Sabha elections and take positions on national issues, so (b).

questions.stem_md: A party keeps no register of members, holds no internal elections, and its top leader takes all decisions. Which challenge does this show?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: No membership register, no organisational elections and decisions by one leader all point to concentrated power inside the party.
Step 2: That is the lack of internal democracy, (d).

questions.stem_md: In a party, the top posts have passed from parent to child for three generations, while long-serving workers have no chance to rise. Which challenge is this?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Leadership is controlled by members of one family.
Step 2: That is dynastic succession, which passes over members without family links, so (c).

questions.stem_md: Parties nominate candidates mainly because they can spend a lot of money or because they have a criminal hold over an area. Which challenge does this show?

options.text_md: Growing role of money and muscle power

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Choosing candidates for their wealth or their power to intimidate shows how money and force shape elections.
Step 2: So (a).

questions.stem_md: Voters complain that the major parties now offer very similar policies, and leaders keep moving from one party to another. Which challenge is this?

options.text_md: Growing role of money and muscle power

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: When ideological differences shrink and leaders switch sides freely, voters cannot find real alternatives.
Step 2: That is the lack of meaningful choice, (b).

questions.stem_md: Under the anti-defection law, what happens to an elected MP or MLA who changes party after the election?

options.text_md: He or she gets a ministerial post.
He or she loses the seat in the legislature.
Nothing; members may change party freely.
He or she must contest the next election as an independent.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The Constitution was amended to stop elected representatives switching parties for personal gain.
Step 2: A member who defects loses the seat, so (b).

questions.stem_md: What has been one **unintended** effect of the anti-defection law?

options.text_md: It has made defections more common.
It has made the party leadership more powerful, since members must accept whatever the leaders decide.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Members can no longer leave the party without losing their seats.
Step 2: So they must follow the leadership, which concentrates power in a few hands, (b).

questions.stem_md: Following a Supreme Court order, what must every candidate file before contesting an election?

options.text_md: A promise to join the ruling party
A certificate of party membership for ten years
A list of all family members in politics
An affidavit giving details of property and of criminal cases pending

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The order aims to reduce the influence of money and crime.
Step 2: Candidates must declare their assets and pending criminal cases in an affidavit, so (d).

questions.stem_md: The Election Commission has required political parties to

options.text_md: hold organisational elections and file income tax returns
give every candidate a government job

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: To improve accountability inside parties, the Commission now requires parties to elect their office-bearers internally and to submit income tax returns.
Step 2: So (a).

questions.stem_md: Which suggested reform aims mainly at reducing the role of **money** in elections?

options.text_md: Reserving one-third of tickets for women
A members' register in every party

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: If the government meets part of the costs of parties' campaigns, candidates need to rely less on wealthy donors.
Step 2: So (a). (c) and (d) address women's representation and internal democracy.

questions.stem_md: Which reform would most directly tackle **dynastic succession**?

options.text_md: Requiring open, regular elections to the highest party posts, supervised by an independent authority

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Dynastic succession happens when top posts are filled by family members without open competition.
Step 2: Open elections to the top posts, fairly supervised, give other members a real chance, so (a).

questions.stem_md: Why do some people warn against too much legal regulation of political parties?

options.text_md: Heavy regulation could be used by the ruling party to control or harm its rivals, and could discourage people from joining politics.
Parties should not have to follow any law.
It would increase internal democracy too much.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Laws on parties are made by parties in power.
Step 2: Too much control may be misused against opponents and may discourage participation, so reforms should be careful: (a).

questions.stem_md: Besides new laws, which is an important way to reform political parties?

options.text_md: Citizens, the media and movements putting pressure on parties, and more people joining parties

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Parties respond to the people who vote for and join them.
Step 2: Public pressure through petitions, publicity and agitation, and the participation of good citizens, can change parties from within, so (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Political parties are necessary in a large representative democracy.

**Reason (R):** Parties bring different representatives together so that a responsible government and clear policies can be formed.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true and explains A: without parties, no one could put together a programme or be held responsible for the government. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A political party is partisan.

**Reason (R):** Parties are registered with the Election Commission.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: a party takes a side and speaks for a section of society.
Step 2: R is true, but registration does not explain why a party is partisan. So (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** China has a two-party system.

**Reason (R):** In China, only the Communist Party is allowed to rule.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is false: China has a one-party system.
Step 2: R is true. So (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** India has a multi-party system.

**Reason (R):** India's social and geographical diversity is not easily absorbed by two or three parties.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true and explains A: the many groups and regions of India produce many parties. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Coalition governments are always more stable than single-party governments.

**Reason (R):** In a coalition, several parties share power.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is false: coalitions can fall if a partner withdraws.
Step 2: R is true. So (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Recognised parties are given a unique election symbol.

**Reason (R):** Only the official candidates of a recognised party may use its reserved symbol.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true, but it describes how the symbol is protected, not why parties are given one. Symbols are given so that voters, many of whom recognise pictures more easily than names, can identify a party's candidates. So (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A party winning 10 per cent of votes and 3 seats in a state assembly election meets the state-party criteria in the syllabus.

**Reason (R):** A state party must win at least 4 seats in the Lok Sabha.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: 10 per cent is above 6 per cent and 3 seats are at least 2.
Step 2: R is false: 4 Lok Sabha seats is part of the national-party criteria. So (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Candidates must declare their assets and pending criminal cases in an affidavit.

**Reason (R):** The aim is to help voters make an informed choice and to reduce the influence of money and crime.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true.
Step 2: R is true and explains A. So (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** After the anti-defection law, elected members are free to vote against their party's decisions without any consequence.

**Reason (R):** The anti-defection law was made by amending the Constitution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is false: members who defy the party in the ways the law covers can lose their seats.
Step 2: R is true. So (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Dynastic succession is unfair to ordinary members of a party.

**Reason (R):** Most political parties hold regular, open elections for their top posts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A is true: members without family links rarely rise to the top.
Step 2: R is false: many parties do not hold open internal elections, which is part of the problem. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Explain the different kinds of party systems. Why has India developed a multi-party system?

3. **Multi-party system**: three or more parties can realistically govern, alone or by **teaming up**; this produces **coalition governments**, as in **India**.

questions.stem_md: Describe the major challenges faced by political parties in India.

3. **Money power**: parties tend to field candidates who can **spend heavily**, and wealthy donors may **influence** policy.
4. **Muscle power**: some parties support candidates with **criminal records** who can win through fear.
5. **Lack of meaningful choice**: differences between major parties have **narrowed**, and leaders **switch parties**, leaving voters with few real alternatives.

3. **Election Commission order**: parties must hold **organisational elections** and file **income tax returns**.

questions.stem_md: After losing an election, Party M's members collect lakhs of signatures and hold street meetings against a rise in electricity tariffs. Which functions are they performing?

options.text_md: Acting as the opposition and shaping public opinion
Forming the government and making laws

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: A losing party that challenges a government decision is acting as the opposition.
Step 2: Petitions and meetings build public awareness, which shapes public opinion. So (a).

questions.stem_md: Why do most candidates in a large national election try to get a party ticket rather than contest as independents?

options.text_md: Independents are not allowed to contest.
A party ticket brings a recognised symbol, an organisation of workers and a programme voters know.
Party candidates do not need any votes.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Independents may contest, but they lack the resources parties provide.
Step 2: A party gives a familiar symbol, workers to campaign and a known programme, which voters use to choose. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Party R won at least 6 per cent of the votes in assembly elections in four states but only 2 Lok Sabha seats. Under the criteria in the syllabus, Party R

options.text_md: qualifies as a national party because of its votes in four states
qualifies as a national party because it has seats in the Lok Sabha
does not qualify as a national party, because it has fewer than 4 Lok Sabha seats

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: The votes condition is met through the four states.
Step 2: The seats condition needs at least 4 Lok Sabha seats; R has 2. Both are needed, so it does not qualify: (d).

questions.stem_md: A proposed law says every party must publish a list of its members and elect its office-bearers every three years under an independent observer. Which challenge does it target?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Member lists and regular internal elections open up the party to its members.
Step 2: That targets the lack of internal democracy, (c).

options.text_md: A minimum share of tickets for women

questions.solution_md:

Step 2: That is the suggested reform of a minimum quota of tickets for women, (a).

questions.stem_md: In a coalition government, a small regional party with only 12 seats threatens to withdraw unless its state gets a special development package. What does this show?

options.text_md: Small parties have no influence in coalitions.
In a coalition, even a small partner can have bargaining power out of proportion to its size.
Regional parties cannot take part in national government.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: If the coalition needs the 12 seats to keep its majority, the small party can make demands.
Step 2: Its bargaining power exceeds its size, which can bring regional concerns forward but also make the government unstable. So (c).

questions.stem_md: Five MLAs of the ruling party vote with the opposition to bring down their own government after being offered posts. Under the anti-defection law, they

options.text_md: can be disqualified and lose their seats

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Voting against the party's direction to bring down its government is the kind of defection the law targets.
Step 2: Such members can be disqualified and lose their seats, so (d).

questions.stem_md: Some people argue that panchayat elections should be held without party symbols. Give one argument for and one against this idea.

answer.model_answer_md: **For**: village issues are **local**, and without party labels voters may judge candidates on **personal record**, reducing **division**. **Against**: without parties, candidates lack an **organisation** and a **programme**, and voters cannot hold any group **responsible**.

questions.solution_md: One argument on each side, linked to what parties do.

questions.stem_md: An unrecognised party's candidate prints posters with a picture very similar to a recognised party's symbol. Why would this be a problem, and how does the recognition system prevent it?

answer.model_answer_md: Voters who identify parties by **symbols** could be **misled** into voting for the wrong candidate. A recognised party's symbol is **reserved**, so **only its official candidates** may use it on the ballot.

questions.solution_md: Explain the confusion and the reservation of symbols.

questions.stem_md: Compare the party systems of the United Kingdom and India, and explain why they differ.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) The **UK** usually has a **two-party** system: two big parties take turns in power. (ii) **India** has a **multi-party** system, with strong **state parties** and frequent **coalitions**. (iii) They differ because party systems **evolve** from each society: India's much greater **social and regional diversity** cannot fit into two parties.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: UK.
Step 2: India.
Step 3: Reason for the difference.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate state funding of elections as a reform: give two benefits and one risk.

answer.model_answer_md: **Benefits**: (i) candidates would depend less on **rich donors**, reducing **money power**; (ii) honest candidates with little money could **compete** more fairly. **Risk**: (iii) parties may still spend **unaccounted money** on top, unless spending limits are **enforced**.

questions.solution_md: Two benefits and one risk, weighed.

questions.stem_md: "Coalition governments have both strengthened and weakened democracy in India." Analyse.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Strengthened**
1. Coalitions brought **state parties** into national government, giving **regional concerns** a voice.
2. The centre had to **consult** partners and **respect the states**, strengthening **federalism**.
3. A **common minimum programme** forced parties to **negotiate** and build consensus.

**Weakened**
4. Governments could **fall** when a partner withdrew, causing **instability** and costly re-elections.
5. Small partners sometimes extracted **concessions** out of proportion to their support, and decisions could be **slow**. On balance, coalitions made democracy more **representative**, though sometimes less **stable**.

questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Three ways coalitions strengthened democracy.
Step 2: Two ways they weakened it.
Step 3: A balanced conclusion.
